items.title: On the Fortune or the Virtue of Alexander by Plutarch
items.description:
Plutarch's "On the Fortune or Virtue of Alexander the Great" is not just a showcase of his rhetorical abilities, but also a revealing insight into his philosophical beliefs. During the Second Sophistic movement, Plutarch challenged traditional concepts of philosophy by questioning whether it was theory or practice that truly defined a philosopher. He used the life and reign of Alexander as a framework to analyze this question.

In addition to analyzing Alexander's life, Plutarch also cast him as
items.why_watch: This is a close reading of a surprisingly underexamined Plutarch text — one where he uses Alexander the Great not as a historical subject but as a philosophical test case for whether virtue can exist without theory. The framing around the Second Sophistic movement gives useful context for why this debate mattered in Plutarch's own moment, not just antiquity. A good listen if you want ancient philosophy that feels genuinely argumentative rather than settled.

items.why_watch: Like Stories of Old uses the quietly devastating film Aftersun to explore how memory doesn't just fade — it actively distorts, filling gaps with feelings we couldn't name at the time. Tom van der Linden's specific insight is that the film's fragmentary structure mirrors how grief works retroactively, reshaping ordinary moments into ones that hurt. Whether or not you've seen the film, this essay will make you think differently about your own half-remembered summers.

items.title: Scientists Just Found a Possible Sign of Life on Saturn's Moon Enceladus
items.description:
Enceladus may look like a frozen moon, but beneath its icy surface could be one of the most mysterious environments in the Solar System. In this video, we take a closer look at Saturn’s moon Enceladus, its strange surface, mysterious cracks, icy terrain, subsurface ocean, water plumes, and the scientific discoveries that continue to surprise researchers.
Why is Enceladus so unusual? What is hiding beneath its frozen crust? Could its underground ocean contain the chemical ingredients necessary fo
items.why_watch: The underlying science — phosphine-like compounds and organic molecules detected in Enceladus's water plumes — is legitimately exciting, but at nearly 60 minutes, this Bright Side video stretches thin material with padding and broad-strokes narration rather than scientific depth. If Enceladus genuinely interests you, you'll get more from a 15-minute NASA explainer or a recent Nature paper summary than from this one.

Wavelet transform is an invaluable tool in signal processing, which has applications in a variety of fields - from hydrodynamics to neuroscience. This revolutionary method allows us to uncover stru
items.why_watch: Artem Kirsanov does something genuinely difficult here: he explains why wavelet transforms outperform Fourier analysis for real-world signals by building the intuition from scratch, using crisp visuals that show what "resolution in both time and frequency" actually means. By the end, you'll understand why wavelets are used in JPEG 2000 compression and neuroscience spike detection — not just that they are. Strong recommend for anyone who nodded along in a signals course without fully believing they understood it.

discovery_articles.title: Cinema Africa in Asmara, Eritrea
discovery_articles.snippet: Built during the Italian colonial era, when Asmara boasted one of the highest concentrations of cinemas in the continent, Cinema Africa belonged to a city where going to the movies was as much a social ritual as an evening's entertainment. Now outside the sightseeing circuit that comprises Cinema Impero and Roma, this building is one of the largest cinemas in the country and a remarkable example of Art Deco architecture that remains largely undiscovered. It still houses a functioning café, accessible through the side entrance, on the ground floor where people gather over espresso and chatter, preserving the atmosphere that once made Asmara's cinemas as much about meeting friends as watching films.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Asmara once had more cinemas per capita than almost anywhere else on the continent — a colonial-era extravagance that left behind Art Deco gems most travelers still walk past without a glance. The fact that one of the largest still serves espresso through a side door, its social heartbeat quietly intact, feels like a secret the city is keeping just for those who look closely enough.

discovery_articles.title: These Coral Reefs Off West Africa Were Long Presumed Dead. Scientists Just Found Them Alive and Teeming With Life
discovery_articles.snippet: Fish surveys in the 1960s detected what experts thought was a dead coral reef barrier off the country of Benin. Decades later, researchers set off in small fishing boats to investigate it using sonar mapping, underwater drone surveys and stationary video recorders
discovery_articles.ferns_note: For roughly sixty years, an entire reef ecosystem off the coast of Benin was written off as dead — filed away in the ledger of ecological loss — until researchers in fishing boats with sonar gear discovered it very much alive. It's a reminder that 'presumed dead' is not the same as gone, and that the ocean still holds corrections to our assumptions.

discovery_articles.title: Avoiding These Three Vascular Health Risk Factors in Midlife Can Help You Delay Dementia for About 13 Years, Study Suggests
discovery_articles.snippet: High blood pressure, diabetes and smoking are three major modifiable risk factors of dementia. New research tracked more than 12,000 participants to quantify how many years of healthy cognitive function you can gain by evading some or all of them during middle age
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Thirteen years of additional healthy cognitive function is not a small number — it's roughly the span between your early fifties and your mid-sixties, rewritten by choices made before the damage compounds. The quiet power of this study is that it puts dementia's timeline, at least partly, back in human hands.

discovery_articles.title: What Spider-Man gets right — and wrong — about turning off superpowers
discovery_articles.snippet: In 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day,' Peter Parker devises a superpower inhibitor based on a real therapy using RNA.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: It turns out the comic-book writers weren't entirely making things up: the superpower inhibitor Peter Parker sketches out mirrors a real RNA-silencing therapy used in actual medicine. The gap between Marvel's fiction and the biology lab is, apparently, thinner than anyone thought to check.

discovery_articles.title: In praise of zealotry
discovery_articles.snippet: Early feminists like Mary Astell and Catharine Macaulay refused their male peers’ advice to remain polite in debate. Why? - by Geertje Bol Read on Aeon
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Mary Astell and Catharine Macaulay were told, as women in early feminist debate, that politeness would earn them more ground — and they refused, loudly, on principle. The argument Geertje Bol makes is that their so-called zealotry wasn't a liability; it was the whole point.

discovery_articles.title: Neurodiversity in the Clinic
discovery_articles.snippet: Autism researcher Patrick Dwyer examines how the neurodiversity movement is influencing autism research and clinical decision-making. The post Neurodiversity in the Clinic appeared first on JSTOR Daily .
discovery_articles.ferns_note: The neurodiversity movement began largely outside clinical walls — in community spaces, online forums, and the lived experience of autistic people themselves — and it is only now reshaping the research and diagnostic frameworks that once excluded those voices entirely. That the clinic is catching up, rather than leading, says something worth sitting with.

discovery_articles.title: Julie Green’s ‘The Last Supper’ Memorializes Hundreds of People’s Final Meals While on Death Row
discovery_articles.snippet: Over a 22-year period, Green illustrated final requests ranging from pizzas and lobster to pies and KFC cartons. Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Over twenty-two years, Julie Green painted hundreds of last meal requests onto dinner plates — and the range is quietly devastating, from lobster to a simple KFC carton, each one a portrait of a person reducing their final wish to something recognizable and human. It is, somehow, both a memorial and an argument.
